    Plays and win-probability swings

      Outcome distributions

      Model check: actual plays vs. predictions

      Before each play the model predicts a full distribution of outcomes. When the play happens, it's scored against that prediction. One play says little because single-play yardage is heavily skewed. But by the central limit theorem, the sum of many play residuals (actual minus expected yards) is close to normal, with variance equal to the sum of each play's variance plus a small correlation term, since plays by the same team share that day's form (measured at ρ = 0.013 across 4,800 games, with no play-to-play momentum). That makes it possible to test whether a team is beating the model by more than chance.

      What if

      Change one assumption and re-simulate from the current spot. The point values are your estimates, not the model's. They move the ND edge and the scoring level the same way the betting line does.

      Backtest on finished games

      Replays real games through the model. At each sampled snap it simulates the rest of the game from that exact spot, then scores the win probability against who actually won, next to ESPN's own number from the same moment. Lower Brier score and log loss are better. Team strength comes from each game's betting line, so this tests the in-game engine, not the line. Timeouts aren't in ESPN's play data, so every replayed snap assumes three each.

      snaps

      Results build up across sessions on this device, so you can add a few game days over time.

      What's going into this

      Player usage comes from each team's 2026 play-by-play so far. Targets on incompletions are read from the play description, so a few unlabeled throws are left out. Penalties are excluded, and injuries or depth chart changes since last week won't show up.

      Live mode fills all of this in from ESPN. Use it when the feed is off or lagging, or to test a spot by hand.
